Neonates of the waterflea Diaphanosoma sarsi emerge from the brood chamber at a total length of 0.063 cm [Lb = 0.063 cm], a size that facilitates their immediate entry into the filter-feeding planktonic community. Following birth, these juvenile crustaceans grow rapidly, an essential life-history strategy for reaching reproductive capacity before the onset of environmental stressors. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 29 °C [T = 29 °C], hatching occurs approximately one day after oviposition, with the age at birth recorded as 1.0 day [ab = 1.0 day]. This brief embryonic period is characteristic of many tropical and subtropical cladocerans, where elevated temperatures accelerate developmental rates. The newborn individuals exhibit a transparent carapace and begin filtering phytoplankton within hours of their release, owing to the rapid resorption of their limited yolk reserves. This early onset of exogenous feeding is critical for sustaining the high growth rates that will ultimately define their adult body dimensions and overall fitness within the zooplankton assemblage.

The onset of sexual maturation in Diaphanosoma sarsi is a tightly constrained developmental milestone that occurs at just 2.62 days [tp = 2.62 days] since birth when individuals are reared at 29 °C [T = 29 °C]. By this point, the growing juvenile attains a distinct total length at puberty of 0.082 cm [Lp = 0.082 cm], signaling the transition to a reproductively viable organism. This remarkably rapid pubertal development, completing in less than three days, reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction under the warm thermal regime typical of subtropical ephemeral ponds. The corresponding size at maturity is intermediate between the neonatal length and the maximum recorded body size for the species, indicating that post-pubertal growth continues as resources are increasingly partitioned toward gamete production. Upon reaching this size threshold, the young crustacean begins to develop the morphological features characteristic of an ovigerous female, such as a fully formed brood chamber, enabling the first reproductive effort to commence almost immediately.

Under the same thermal conditions of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the lifespan of Diaphanosoma sarsi from birth to natural death extends to approximately 23 days [am = approximately 23 days]. This longevity is relatively brief, but it encompasses a full reproductive schedule for the species. Over the course of this adult life, a single female releases a total of 88 neonates, yielding a maximum reproductive rate of approximately 4.3 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 4.3 offspring per day], calculated by dividing the lifetime neonate output by the reproductive period spanning from 2.62 days to 23 days of age. This high daily fecundity is a hallmark of opportunistic, r-selected planktonic crustaceans that exploit transient resource pulses. The ability to sustain such an output relies on a continuous conversion of ingested algal biomass into offspring, a process that is energetically demanding but highly effective in rapid population expansion during favorable seasons. The total lifetime neonate production of 88 young ensures that, even with high early mortality in the planktonic environment, a sufficient number of individuals survive to sustain the population.

When scanning electron microscopy and dry mass determinations are performed on fully grown adults, the ultimate dry weight of Diaphanosoma sarsi is estimated at 23.1 micrograms . This value, derived from allometric scaling relationships with larger daphniids, underscores the minute but functionally significant biomass of these suspension feeders in the pelagic zone. Concurrently, the ultimate total length attained by these ovigerous adults reaches 0.125 cm [Li = 0.125 cm], representing a near doubling of the length recorded at puberty. This final body size is a critical determinant of the brood chamber volume and, consequently, the maximum clutch size that an individual can accommodate. The allometric increase from approximately 0.082 cm at maturity to 0.125 cm reflects a pronounced investment in somatic growth even during the reproductive phase, allowing older females to chamber more developing eggs and thereby contribute disproportionately to population recruitment.

Population-level surveys of Diaphanosoma sarsi in subtropical water bodies reveal that the species' demographic dynamics are closely tied to the thermal regime. At 29 °C [T = 29 °C], the compressed developmental schedule described above yields a generation time of roughly 24 days, driven by the precise maturation timeline.
